gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Goal Zero's own page for the current ("New") Sherpa 100AC lists its USB-C Power Delivery ports at "60 Watts each" next to an "Integrated 100W AC" outlet. ChatGPT's answers and our current table both say the Sherpa 100AC has "100W USB-C". For a laptop that needs more than 60 W, that changes whether the shopper should use the USB-C port or the AC outlet on this bank.
standout_why: I compared against our page (dealectric.com, cited) and geekchamp.com (cited). Our page gives 100 W USB-C and calls the Sherpa's inverter modified sine. ChatGPT repeated the '100W USB-C' figure from our page. Geekchamp says only that pure sine matters for CPAP and similar loads; it states no waveform for the Sherpa and says the Sherpa's continuous AC wattage is not given. Neither page has Goal Zero's 60 W-per-port wording for the new model. I couldn't open gearlark.com (TLS certificate error). I didn't read Engadget, Macworld, Wired or the other results because of the call budget, so I can't say whether one of them has the 60 W figure. That uncertainty is why the score is 2 and not 3.
decides: This doesn't change the Sherpa 100AC as the flight-legal pick (95 Wh, 2-year warranty, $249.95 at Goal Zero today). It does change the advice and the table. We should stop printing '100 W USB-C' for the new Sherpa 100AC unless Goal Zero's full spec table says otherwise. For laptops that draw 60 W or less, use USB-C and skip the inverter; our page already cites a test where only about 70% of a battery reached the laptop over AC. Bigger laptops would have to use the 100 W AC outlet with that loss, or go to a station. The waveform claim (modified sine) needs a source before it goes back on the page, because Goal Zero's store labels its Yeti inverters 'pure sine wave' but the Sherpa text I could read gives no waveform.
